shape.name: Shape F - Productive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional productive skills lesson with preparation stages followed by speaking or writing output.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Here the focus is on helping learners practice their speaking or writing skills. The lesson can usually be divided into preparation for speaking/writing and speaking/writing task stages.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to [speak/write] about [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to plan a for-and-against essay by organizing ideas into advantages and disadvantages, reducing their notes, and ordering their strongest points.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
09-08-26
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
F (Productive Skills - Writing)
Materials:
Textbook writing workshop pp. 133-134, slideshow, essay topic cards, planning worksheet
Assessment:
Completed essay plan (for/against notes, ordered)
Skills:
Writing

stages.stage_aim: To reactivate lesson 1 and set the theme: today we plan the essay from both sides of our topic
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: "What do you see? Sticky notes and a whiteboard. What might this lesson be about?" Let students guess.
Advance to the title slide: "Plan your ideas." Confirm the theme: today we plan the for/against essay.
Show the "Why is this lesson important?" slide and read the bullets aloud.
Pairs recap lesson 1: "Which side did you choose? Tell your partner." Students restate their card and their position.
Point to the Opinion-Reason-Evidence line at the bottom of the slide.

stages.stage_aim: To teach the organizing strategy: one paragraph for advantages, one for disadvantages
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Organize your ideas."
Teach the strategy table: put the advantages in one paragraph, then the disadvantages in another.
Check understanding: Which paragraph shows the good points? Which shows the bad points?

stages.stage_aim: To generate many points for each side and match notes to topics (Exercise 2)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Generate ideas."
Teach the strategy table: think of many points for each side; think of people you know.
Exercise 2 on page 133: students match the four notes (a-d) to the essay topics and say if each is for or against.
Reveal the answers row by row: a, b and d are advantages; c is a disadvantage.

stages.stage_aim: To teach note reduction and apply it (Exercise 3)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Take short notes."
Teach the strategy table: cut words, keep only the key information.
Run the demo: cut "it helps you practice speaking English at home" to "helps practice English".
Exercise 3 on page 133: students reduce the notes to the word counts, then check the answers row by row.

stages.stage_aim: For students to write their arguments in the For/Against table and add counter-arguments (Exercise 4)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Plan your essay."
Project the Exercise 4 task slide on page 134.
Students write their arguments in the For (Advantages) and Against (Disadvantages) columns, then add what another person might say in answer. 5 minutes (timer).
Monitor: both columns must have ideas.

stages.stage_aim: To teach selecting and ordering the strongest ideas, using the model essay (Exercise 6)
procedure: Teach the strategy table: choose the strongest ideas; you have space for only two or three.
Reveal the Exercise 6 answers: which arguments are joined in one sentence, which paragraph begins with the strongest argument, and which ends with the strongest point.
Ask: should you start or finish each paragraph with your strongest point?

stages.stage_aim: For pairs to test their arguments and for students to select and order their own notes
procedure: Exercise 5 on page 134: students read one column of their arguments to a partner.
The partner makes an opposite argument for each point.
Exercise 6 question 4: students select their strongest ideas and order them for each paragraph. 6 minutes (timer).
Collect the plans at the end of the stage.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the plan and preview lesson 3: drafting
procedure: Show the wrap-up slide: "Your plan is ready."
Preview lesson 3: writing the introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion from the plan.

shape.note: For middle schoolers interested in SCR approach to productive skills, see Shape J instead.

metadata.topic: For and against essays: think and plan
materials: Oxford Discover Futures 2, Unit "Writing workshop: A for and against essay", pp. 133–134
Essay topic cards — each student's assigned topic from Lesson 1
Essay planning worksheet — For (Advantages) / Against (Disadvantages) table (Exercise 4)
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to plan a for-and-against essay by organizing ideas into advantages and disadvantages, reducing their notes, and ordering their strongest points.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also be better able to match notes to essay topics and identify whether a point is for or against a technology.
answer_key: a It saves the cutting down of trees — reading books on digital devices (for).
b It encourages people to have social interaction — social media (for).
c There's a lack of feedback from a teacher — studying online (against).
d You can meet and play with new people — online gaming (for).
1 saves cutting down trees, or saves trees.

1 Paragraph 2 joins two ideas in one sentence: "Second, you can create your own playlists, and what's more, share them with friends easily." Paragraph 3 does the same: "There's also the fact that some artists don't appear on streaming services, and another argument against them is that they don't pay artists much."
2 Paragraph 2 begins with the strongest argument: "First, and most importantly, streaming means you can listen to your favorite songs anywhere, on any device, without using up memory on it."
3 Paragraph 3 ends with the strongest disadvantage: "Last but not least, when you stream music, unfortunately you don't own it at all."
